vis.title: Learning is insight,
vis.sub: Rajan Kumar V K · Teaching philosophy

segs.text: I am Rajan Kumar V K. I have taught for more than ten years, first in school science laboratories in Nepal, and then at LUT University in Finland.
My teaching rests on four principles. The first is clarity. A complex idea should be made simple, without losing its meaning.
The second is relevance. Students learn best when they see why knowledge matters, so I bring real industrial problems, and my own research, into the classroom.
The third is a student-centred environment, where people feel safe to ask, to doubt, and to try.
The fourth is the one closest to me. Learning is insight, not accumulation. Fear suppresses curiosity. Freedom to question is where understanding begins.
So my role is to guide, not to dominate. I ask before I tell.

eyebrow: A physics lesson from my school classroom

vis.note: A bottle of water with holes near the base

segs.text: A rooftop in Nepal. A class of fifteen year olds. In my hand, a plastic bottle full of water, with holes near the bottom. Water streams out.
I tell them: if Einstein is right, the water will stop the moment I let go. Before anything happens, every student must predict.
Then I release the bottle. For the whole fall, the streams vanish.

ask: No weight pressing on the holes
Free fall feels like no gravity

segs.text: Why? The bottle and the water fall together. Inside the falling bottle, the water has no weight to push it out. That is free fall, and it is the heart of Einstein's equivalence principle.
Predict, observe, explain. A physics lesson that costs one bottle, and that nobody forgets.

eyebrow: Teaching system-level thinking to civil engineering students

vis.title: One building,
vis.sub: System-level thinking for civil engineering students

segs.text: How would I teach civil engineering students in their first years? I would start with one decision.
A concrete building from the nineteen seventies. Four options. Repair the minimum, renovate deeply, convert it to a new use, or demolish and build new.
Students examine each option through four lenses: technical condition, business cost over the life cycle, environmental impact, and the effect on the people who use the building.
Then they change seats. The owner, the user, the city and the contractor weigh those lenses differently, and the best option changes with them.

vis.text: No single right answer. A well-argued one.

segs.text: There is no single right answer. There is a well-argued one. That is system-level thinking, and it is what the profession will need.

eyebrow: Mentoring in the Lahti Venture Program

vis.title: From a question
vis.sub: A Lahti Venture team and the Kempower challenge

segs.text: In the Lahti Venture Program at LUT University, student teams from different disciplines solve a real problem for a real company. I am their mentor.

vis.head: The challenge
items: How to attract and keep Generation Z talent?
all: How to attract and keep Generation Z talent?

segs.text: Our company was Kempower, a Finnish maker of electric vehicle chargers. The challenge: how can Kempower attract and keep talent from Generation Z?

vis.text: What do you expect from an employer?

segs.text: I did not hand the team a framework. They were Generation Z themselves, so I asked what they expect from an employer. Their own answers became the first hypothesis.

Then the team planned its evidence. Surveys and interviews with students and young professionals. A comparison with other technology companies. An analysis of themes, strengths and gaps. And finally a proposal: an employer value proposition built for Generation Z.
Purpose, growth, flexibility and openness came through as the themes that matter. And a company working on clean transport has a real story to tell on the first of them.
The ideas belonged to the students. My part was to ask, to structure, and to protect the space in which ideas can appear.
